# The register rules: Beli

*A letter to a colleague, 31 July 2026 — on the name Beli, and on the forms that keep failing it.*

Your note said, roughly: surely the marks are a nicety. Permit me to use Beli to show they are not.

First, the attestation. The tradition's record preserves this name in its romanized scholarly form: **Beli** — no older script survives to transcribe, so the canonical content is the exactness of the spelling itself.

Say it aloud as the sources heard it: bEL-ee — two syllables, stress on the first; the e is the open e of 'bed', never the long ay of 'bailey'. The marks are what carry that sound to a reader who has never heard it spoken.

On the plain form — and I want to be precise, because you pushed on this. The plain form *beli* differs from the canonical *Beli* only by convention of display — case, not content. It is *acceptable everywhere*: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

One more thing, because it always surprises: the name did not stay home. Beli's whole cross-cultural argument is the Belenos question.  The continental god is attested from Aquileia to Noricum, glossed by the ancients as a Celtic Apollo, and derived by tradition from *bhel-, 'to shine'.

And it never stopped working. Beli's afterlife is genealogical before it is literary.  The medieval pedigrees made descent from Beli Mawr the deepest claim a British dynasty could print, and the convention outlived the Middle Ages: Tudor and Stuart antiquaries, eager to trace the crown to British and Trojan roots, found Beli waiting at the root of the trees Geoffrey had Latinized.

## The Convention's Own History

Every tradition in this register has its own scholarly transliteration standard, built by its own specialists over decades or centuries, and the register follows each on its own terms: the tradition’s own standard. The principle that unifies them is the one the whole project stands on: a name is evidence, and evidence is not negotiable — not for keyboards, not for convenience, not for anyone.

## Where Protocol Meets Practice

The technical answer is simple: the canonical marks are legal IDNA 2008 characters, encoded as punycode under `xn--`. The practical answer is messier: legal does not mean stocked (registrar inventory is partial), and stocked does not mean typeable (stacked diacritics defeat mobile keyboards).

So the register's rule is a hierarchy of attested forms — full restoration, circumflex, macron-only, attested variant, and finally plain ASCII for the systems that cannot carry marks. Every rung is defensible because every rung is attested. The forms this register rules against are not rungs; they are errors, and errors do not get rungs.

Write back when you have checked the sources; they are better company than I am.

*— The Register*

## The Verdict

**Beli** is the canonical form: attested, checkable, and enforced across the temple, the lexicon, the cards, the APIs, and this register. The plain form *beli* shares that standing — the two are the same name in every system. The false forms above are documented so that no reader has to take the temple's word on faith — the violations are stated, the sources are named, and the register stands open to challenge on every line.

The temple of **Beli** stands at [/beli/](/beli/).

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 7 cited sources — Mabinogion (Lludd a Llefelys; Branwen ferch Llŷr) — Sioned Davies, The Mabinogion (Oxford), Harleian Genealogies (BL Harley MS 3859) — Peter C. Bartrum, Early Welsh Genealogical Tracts, Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae (Heli, father of Lud, Cassibelaunus, Nennius).
